clue.text: First clue regularly penned by little object of desire for 9

indicators.note: something penned by another is shut inside it, as if in a pen

parts.note: a bit is a little amount

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter at a steady interval through the words

parts.note: the even letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A setter teasing that the opening clue holds a small something that a later answer longs for.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points across the grid to 9-down, the Sesame Street puppet, so the answer is the thing he craves.
explanation.definitionFit: Cookie Monster is the Sesame Street puppet obsessed with cookies, which British English calls biscuits.

clue.text: International gallery without frame for Modigliani copy

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the first pieces sit around the next

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for international

indicators.note: a frame is the outer edge of a picture, so only the outermost letters of the painter's name are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of the painter's name
the Tate is the London art gallery

explanation.surface: A gallery forging a Modigliani and hanging it unframed.
explanation.walkthrough: I and TATE together stand outside MI: I-MI-TATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To imitate is to copy, both as verbs meaning reproduce someone else's work or manner.

clue.text: Colour of carbon paper

parts.note: C is the chemical symbol for carbon
a ream is a quantity of paper, 500 sheets

explanation.surface: Asking what shade carbon paper comes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Cream is a pale yellowish-white shade, named after the top of milk.

clue.text: Footballers in local street upset little kids

indicators.note: in places the football body inside the word for a pub

parts.note: a local is a neighbourhood pub, an inn
the FA is the Football Association, English football's governing body

indicators.note: in a down clue, upset means turned upside down, so the abbreviation reads bottom to top

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Footballers drinking in the pub upsetting the children in the street.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Local' looks like an adjective for the street, but it is the British word for a neighbourhood pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Infants are babies and toddlers, the youngest of little children.

clue.text: Scorcese's gutted with prize for direction of The Deep

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, leaving just the two ends of the name

parts.note: the first and last letters of the director's name
an award is a prize

explanation.surface: Martin Scorsese is gutted that an award went to the director of a film called The Deep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Direction' suggests film directing, but it means a compass heading: the deep is the sea. The clue prints the director's name as Scorcese.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaward means towards the sea, and the deep is a poetic name for the ocean.

clue.text: Jolly English opener on top of other side

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
the verso is the back, or left-hand page, of a sheet

explanation.surface: An English opening batsman getting the better of the opposing team.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, E sits on top of VERSO. 'Jolly' is the British intensifier, as in jolly good.
explanation.definitionFit: Jolly and ever so are both informal British intensifiers meaning very.

clue.text: Top-drawer treatment for a tear

indicators.note: a treatment works material over, so these letters are processed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: First-class care given to a rip, or perhaps to someone crying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' looks like a rip, as in a garment, but it is the kind you cry.
explanation.definitionFit: A tear is a single drop of the salty water the eye produces.

clue.text: Butterfly in part of Barnet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a common brown butterfly with ring-shaped eyespots
second meaning: a curl, Barnet being rhyming slang for hair

explanation.surface: A butterfly spotted in Barnet, a borough of north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet looks like the London borough, but it is Cockney rhyming slang: Barnet Fair means hair.
explanation.definitionFit: The ringlet is a British butterfly species, and a ringlet is also a long spiral curl of hair.

clue.text: Muppet took no mercies unfortunately

indicators.note: something that has gone unfortunately has gone wrong, so the words are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Muppet that sadly showed no mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Muppet' is also British slang for a fool, but here it is the puppet itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Cookie Monster is one of Jim Henson's Muppets, the blue creature from Sesame Street.

clue.text: Sweet counter in Picturehouse cinema

indicators.note: counter means running the opposite way, so the letters are read right to left
in says the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Sweets sold at the snack counter of a Picturehouse cinema.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet counter' reads as a confectionery stand; the counter is the reversal signal. Picturehouse is a British cinema chain.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet and nice are synonyms for pleasant; a Nice biscuit fits the puzzle's biscuit theme too.

clue.text: Learning new technique initially in fine art school

indicators.note: in places the preceding pieces inside the word for fine

parts.note: taken as written; the next pieces go inside it

indicators.note: initially points to taking just the opening letter of technique

parts.note: lore is accumulated learning
N is the abbreviation for new
the opening letter

explanation.surface: Learning a new technique, beginning at a fine art school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine art school' looks like one phrase, but fine is wordplay and only 'art school' defines.
explanation.definitionFit: The Florentine school was the Renaissance painting tradition of Florence; a florentine is also a biscuit.

clue.text: Stop blokes getting Brahms and Liszt?

parts.note: to bar is to stop or block
blokes are men

explanation.surface: A plea to stop men from getting drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: Brahms and Liszt is Cockney rhyming slang for pissed, meaning drunk. The definition is cryptic: barmen are the ones getting you that way, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Bar staff serve the alcohol, so playfully they are the people getting customers drunk.

clue.text: Film star taking odds on golfer making birdies

parts.note: Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel

indicators.note: taking means removing, so the odd-placed letters go and the even ones remain

parts.note: the second and fourth letters
Ernie Els is the South African golfer

explanation.surface: A film star placing a bet on a golfer to make birdies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birdies' suggests golf scores, but it means small birds.
explanation.definitionFit: Kestrels are small falcons, so birdies in the informal sense of birds.

clue.text: Nova Scotia saving energy with revolutionary selenium insulators?

indicators.note: saving means keeping hold of, so the province's name holds the next letter
nova is Latin for new, so the letters are made into something new

parts.note: taken as written
E is the symbol for energy

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the chemical symbol is read backwards

parts.note: Se is the chemical symbol for selenium

explanation.surface: Nova Scotia conserving energy by using a new selenium-based insulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nova Scotia' reads as the Canadian province, but Nova is the anagram signal for SCOTIA plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea cosies are padded covers that keep a teapot warm, so whimsically they are insulators.

clue.text: Constant thick fog ruined contest

indicators.note: something ruined has been wrecked, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: c is the symbol for a constant, such as the speed of light
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture abandoned because of persistent thick fog.
explanation.definitionFit: A cockfight is a contest between two gamecocks, staged for betting.

clue.text: German guy in F1

parts.note: surface reading: a German racing driver in Formula One
setter's reading: the stock nickname for a German man

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the traditional slang name for a German; its last four letters spell a cracker brand, matching the puzzle's biscuit theme, but how 'in F1' contributes is not clear.
explanation.definitionFit: Fritz, a common German forename, became British and American slang for any German man.

clue.text: First sign of Steve Cram getting beaten

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter
to cram food in is to tuck in; tuck is also British slang for food

explanation.surface: Steve Cram, the British middle-distance runner, showing the first sign of losing a race.
explanation.walkthrough: Steve Cram is a former British miler, but his surname is wordplay for stuffing food.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuck means stumped or defeated by a problem, so beaten in the sense of baffled.

clue.text: Prime Minister kind of cross about being short?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the cross wraps round the next word

parts.note: a tau cross is T-shaped, named after the Greek letter
being short with someone is being curt, or rude

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister getting cross about being called short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is a shape of cross.
explanation.definitionFit: Pierre and Justin Trudeau, father and son, both served as Prime Minister of Canada.

clue.text: Flower posies arranged by coroner

indicators.note: arranged, as with flowers in a vase, means put into a new order

parts.note: Cor. is a dictionary abbreviation for coroner
these letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Bunches of flowers laid out by a coroner, perhaps at an inquest.
explanation.walkthrough: The abbreviation COR comes first even though coroner is last in the clue: 'by' means beside.
explanation.definitionFit: Coreopsis, or tickseed, is a yellow daisy-like garden flower.

clue.text: One putting out European champion

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European
a victor is a winner, a champion

explanation.surface: A European champion, perhaps a cricketer, getting a batsman out.
explanation.definitionFit: An evictor removes tenants from a property, so is one who puts people out.

clue.text: Damaged urinals getting closed

indicators.note: damaged things are broken, so these letters are smashed and reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Vandalised public toilets being shut down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Closed' looks like shut, but here it means closed-minded.
explanation.definitionFit: Insular means inward-looking and narrow, like a closed mind cut off from outside ideas.

clue.text: Queen singer holding one more flush

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the queen and singer clasp the number between them

parts.note: R for regina, Latin for queen
I is the Roman numeral one
Cher is the American pop singer

explanation.surface: The singer from the band Queen, Freddie Mercury perhaps, holding a winning poker hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen singer' reads as the rock band's vocalist, but splits into two pieces either side of I.
explanation.definitionFit: Flush is slang for having plenty of money, so more flush means wealthier.

clue.text: Heart of Clement Freud is broken in Scottish town

indicators.note: broken pieces are reassembled in a different order
the heart of a word is its middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of the seven
taken as written

explanation.surface: Clement Freud, the broadcaster and politician, heartbroken while in a Scottish town.
explanation.walkthrough: Clement Freud was a British broadcaster, writer and Liberal MP, grandson of Sigmund.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumfries is a market town in south-west Scotland, home of Robert Burns in later life.

clue.text: Hello! about to claim politician is naughty

indicators.note: to claim is to take in, so the greeting surrounds the next pieces
about means turned round, so the greeting is read backwards

parts.note: hi is a greeting
MP is a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: Hello! magazine about to make a claim that a politician is being naughty.
explanation.walkthrough: Hello! is a British celebrity magazine; here it just gives a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Impish means mischievous like an imp, so playfully naughty.

clue.text: Person somewhat left out

indicators.note: out means removed, so that letter is dropped from the word

parts.note: partly means somewhat, to some degree
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone feeling a bit left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove L from PARTLY.
explanation.definitionFit: In legal and formal usage a party is a person involved, as in the guilty party.

clue.text: Most tedious restoration of The Elgin Marbles finally ahead of time

indicators.note: restoration rebuilds something, so these letters are put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the word before it

parts.note: the last letter
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Restoring the Elgin Marbles, the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum, is the most drawn-out business of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Lengthiest means going on longest, so the most wearisome and tedious.

clue.text: Register of vocal part

indicators.note: vocal means spoken out, so it is the sound of the next word that counts

parts.note: an actor's part is a role

explanation.surface: The register for the vocal part, as in singing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Register' and 'vocal part' both suggest singing ranges, but register is a list of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A roll is an official list of names, as in a school register or electoral roll.

clue.text: Roland Rat successfully holding back pink cat

indicators.note: back means read in the opposite direction
holding means the letters are contained within the words before it

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of Roland to the start of successfully

explanation.surface: Roland Rat, the 1980s TV puppet, managing to restrain a pink cat.
explanation.walkthrough: Roland Rat was a puppet star of British breakfast TV; he only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Custard is the pink cat in the British cartoon Roobarb and Custard, and also custard creams in the biscuit theme.

clue.text: Jets ignoring leader of Sharks' appeals

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so that letter is dropped

parts.note: jets of water come from sprayers

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: The New York Jets losing out to a rival side, the Sharks, on appeals.
explanation.walkthrough: Jets and Sharks are the rival gangs in West Side Story; neither is meant literally.
explanation.definitionFit: Prayers are earnest requests addressed to God, so appeals or entreaties.
